title: The Ice Ages, What the Ice Left Behind
description: Tonight is about ice, and about what ice leaves behind. Not the ice itself, which is gone from nearly every place it once lay, but the traces: a hillside in Sicily with a dark layer in it, a core of mud from the bottom of the sea, a bubble of very old air, a boulder on a prairie, a shoreline on a mountainside above a salt flat, a cliff of wind-blown dust, and a single line in a column of Greenland ice. It runs from about two and a half million years ago to about eleven thousand seven hundred years ago, the formal start of the epoch we live in now, and it ends on a look back across the whole of it.

It is told through places and traces rather than through creatures. The large animals of the ice age are not in it, and neither is anyone who lived then. The cast is stone, mud, ice, air, water and the smallest traces of plants.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. What started the great ice in the north, whether the orbit of the Earth is the pacemaker of the ice or only a nudge, why the beat of the ice changed about a million years ago, how low the sea fell, what the word "ice age" should mean, and even a counting slip of 99 years against 69 at the base of the present epoch are all argued over, or differ between the pages. Where the sources disagree the episode says so aloud and keeps the voices apart.
It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and no one is harmed in the telling.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the line in the Greenland ice, that's the intended use.

accuracy: Every factual claim traces to a named source, condensed below to those the narration leans on most. Where sources disagree, the episode gives both views. Many could only be read as abstracts, summaries or digests, and a few were behind bot checks and were not read; the narration says so aloud, and the list marks the thinner ones.
